clips.caption:
A plane doesn't ease onto the runway - it goes full throttle, wheels down, for the entire climb.

Kevin Trudeau says a business is the same. In the beginning you put in everything - full effort, long hours, nothing coming back yet - just like a pilot burning fuel just to get the wheels off the ground.

Most people quit right there, in the climb, because it isn't paying off yet. But once you reach cruising altitude, you pull back the throttle and hit autopilot. That's when the business starts working for you instead of the other way around.

The hard part isn't permanent. It's just first.

clips.caption:
Todd Graves wanted to open a chicken restaurant. Nobody would fund it, so he found the money the hard way.

Kevin Trudeau tells it straight: Graves worked 90-hour weeks at an oil refinery, saved every dollar, then went to Alaska to fish for salmon when the refinery work slowed down. He slept on the floor to keep saving.

That restaurant became Raising Cane's. Todd Graves is now worth over $9 billion.

The lesson isn't the chicken. It's that he was willing to do the ugly, unglamorous work everyone else refuses - and that's what actually funded the dream.

What's the unglamorous work you've been avoiding?

#kevintrudeau #entrepreneur #successstory #hustle #businessmindset #wealthmindset

Same house. Same buyers driving by. One realtor couldn't sell it in six months. Another sold it in a week.

Kevin Trudeau says the difference wasn't the market - it was Josh Altman, a Beverly Hills realtor whose company does over a billion and a half a year. He took new pictures, staged the empty rooms, rewrote the listing, and changed the walkthrough completely.

Most realtors narrate: "this is the living room, notice the carpet." Altman asks questions instead - where are you from, what do you do, what's bringing you here - and builds a connection before he ever mentions square footage.

People don't buy a room. They buy a feeling about themselves in it.
